# 1 Measurement, the Business Cycle and the Phillips Curve

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The finals paper draws **30% from the material taught before the midterm**, **35% from M3** and **35% from M4**. The review guide itself only sets out the post-midterm content, so this chapter collects the pre-midterm ideas the practice paper still tests: how output and unemployment are measured, what a business cycle is, and the short-run relationship between inflation and unemployment. Everything from chapter 2 onwards is the post-midterm material.

## Leakages from the circular flow

A **leakage** is spending that drains out of the domestic circular flow rather than returning to domestic firms as income. Of consumer spending, government spending, investment spending and imports, only **imports** are a leakage. The reason follows from what an import is: goods produced abroad and sold domestically, so the money spent on them goes to a foreign producer and leaves the domestic flow. The other three are all payments made to domestic firms, so they stay inside it.

## Value added

**Value added** for a firm is the firm's **sales minus the cost of inputs purchased from other firms**. Note what it is not: it is not sales minus depreciation, not sales minus losses, and not simply the firm's profits from its sales.

## The business cycle

**Business cycles** are **each comprised of a recession and an expansion**. Three things students are commonly caught on:

- they do **not** occur infrequently in capitalist economies;
- they are **not** predictable ups and downs in economic activity;
- they have nothing to do with reusing resources in production.

Recession is the half of the cycle that the recessionary gap of 2.2 and the fiscal expansion of 3.1 respond to.

## Measured unemployment

The **official unemployment rate understates** the true level of unemployment in the economy, because it **ignores underemployed and discouraged workers**. Neither of these groups shows up as unemployed in the official figure, yet both represent labour that the economy is not using.

The other explanations offered for the understatement do not work: the official rate does not fail because it ignores the duration of unemployment, it does not include jobs created by the underground economy, and it does not exclude the frictionally unemployed.

## The short-run Phillips curve

The **short-run Phillips curve** shows a **trade-off between the unemployment rate and the rate of inflation**. Be precise about which unemployment rate: it is not a trade-off between the *natural* rate of unemployment and inflation, and it is not a relationship between increases in the money supply and the rate of inflation.

This trade-off is why a central bank's two goals — keeping inflation within target and maximising employment (2.1) — pull against each other in the short run.

**An increase in input prices produces a rightward shift in the short-run Phillips curve.** It does not shift the money supply curve right, does not shift aggregate demand right, and does not shift short-run aggregate supply right.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Leakage** | Spending that drains out of the circular flow; of the standard components, imports are the leakage |
| **Value added** | A firm's sales minus the cost of inputs purchased from other firms |
| **Business cycle** | A cycle each comprised of a recession and an expansion; not predictable, and not infrequent in capitalist economies |
| **Official unemployment rate** | The published unemployment rate, which understates unemployment because it ignores underemployed and discouraged workers |
| **Short-run Phillips curve** | A curve showing the trade-off between the unemployment rate and the rate of inflation; an increase in input prices shifts it rightward |

# 2.1 Money and the Banking System

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Why money exists

Without money, trade would require **barter**: the exchange of one good or service for another. Every transaction would then require a **double coincidence of wants** — the unlikely occurrence that two people each have a good the other wants. Most people would spend a great deal of time searching for others to trade with, which is a huge waste of resources. Money makes that search unnecessary, and that is the whole economic case for it.

## The three functions of money

| Function | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Medium of exchange** | An item buyers give to sellers when they want to purchase goods and services |
| **Unit of account** | The yardstick people use to post prices and record debts |
| **Store of value** | An item people can use to transfer purchasing power from the present to the future |

## The two types of money

**Commodity money** takes the form of a commodity with **intrinsic value** — gold coins, or cigarettes in prisoner-of-war camps. It would still be worth something if nobody used it as money.

**Fiat money** has **no intrinsic value** and is used as money because of government decree. A US dollar bill is the standard example: the paper is worthless, and the note circulates because the government says it is money.

## The money supply

The **money supply**, or money stock, is **the quantity of money available in the economy**. Two of its ingredients need defining first:

- **Currency** — the paper bills and coins in the hands of the (non-bank) public
- **Demand deposits** — balances in bank accounts that depositors can access on demand by writing a cheque

The guide measures the money supply two ways, one nested inside the other:

| Measure | Contents |
|---|---|
| **M1** | Currency, demand deposits, traveller's cheques, and other chequeable deposits |
| **M2** | Everything in M1, plus savings deposits, small time deposits, money market mutual funds, and a few minor categories |

## The central bank

A **central bank** is an institution that oversees the banking system and regulates the money supply. It has **two main goals**: to keep inflation within target, and to maximise employment. Beyond those goals it plays three standing roles:

- **Regulator of commercial banks** — supervising and regulating commercial banks to ensure financial stability, prevent risky behaviour and protect depositors
- **Banker to government** — managing the government's accounts, helping to issue debt such as bonds, and sometimes financing public spending indirectly
- **Bank's bank, the lender of last resort to banks** — providing emergency liquidity to commercial banks to prevent bank runs and systemic collapse

**Monetary policy** is the setting of the money supply by policymakers in the central bank. The **Federal Reserve (the Fed)** is the central bank of the United States.

*Worked example.* Which of the following is **not** a function of the Fed: setting reserve requirements for banks, advising Congress on fiscal policy, regulating the money supply, or serving as a lender of last resort? The answer is **advising Congress on fiscal policy**. Reserve requirements, the money supply and lender-of-last-resort lending are all listed above as central-bank business; fiscal policy is set by government policymakers, not by the central bank (3.1).

## The structure of the Fed

- The **Board of Governors**, seven members, in Washington, DC
- **12 regional Federal Reserve banks** located around the United States
- The **Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)**, which includes the Board of Governors and the presidents of some of the regional Fed banks, and which **decides monetary policy**

*Worked example.* Which group votes on the open-market operations used to control the US money supply and interest rates? Not "the Fed" in general and not the Board of Governors on its own, but the **FOMC** — it is the committee the guide names as the body that decides monetary policy.

## Bank reserves

In a **fractional reserve banking system**, banks keep a fraction of deposits as **reserves** and use the rest to make loans. The Fed establishes **reserve requirements**: regulations on the minimum amount of reserves that banks must hold against deposits. Banks may hold more than this minimum if they want to.

The **reserve ratio, $R$**, is the fraction of deposits that banks hold as reserves — total reserves as a percentage of total deposits.

$$R = \frac{\text{total reserves}}{\text{total deposits}}$$

Reserves held above the required minimum are **excess reserves**, and they are the funds a bank can actually lend out.

*Worked example.* A commercial bank has \$100 million in chequeable-deposit liabilities and \$12 million in actual reserves, and the required reserve ratio is 10 per cent. How big are the bank's excess reserves? Required reserves are $0.10 \times \$100\text{m} = \$10\text{m}$, so excess reserves are $\$12\text{m} - \$10\text{m} = \$2$ million.

## The bank T-account

A **T-account** is a simplified accounting statement that shows a bank's assets and liabilities. Banks' liabilities include **deposits**; their assets include **loans and reserves**.

*Worked example — Sewell Bank.* The bank's simplified balance sheet is:

| Assets | | Liabilities | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Required reserves | \$2,000 | Demand deposits | \$10,000 |
| Excess reserves | \$0 | Owner's equity | \$10,000 |
| Customer loans | \$8,000 | | |
| Government securities (bonds) | \$7,000 | | |
| Building and fixtures | \$3,000 | | |

**(a) Calculate the required reserve ratio.** The requirement is set against deposits, so divide required reserves by demand deposits: $\$2{,}000 / \$10{,}000 = 0.2$, or **20%**.

**(b) The Federal Reserve purchases \$5,000 worth of bonds from Sewell Bank. What happens immediately to (i) excess reserves and (ii) demand deposits?**

- **(i) Excess reserves increase by \$5,000.** The Fed pays for the bonds with new reserves, and because no new deposits have been created, none of that \$5,000 is required — all of it is excess.
- **(ii) Demand deposits do not change: zero.** The bank has swapped one asset (bonds) for another (reserves). Nobody has deposited anything, so the liabilities side is untouched.

An open-market purchase from a *bank* therefore changes the composition of that bank's assets, not its deposits.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Barter** | The exchange of one good or service for another |
| **Double coincidence of wants** | The unlikely occurrence that two people each have a good the other wants |
| **Medium of exchange** | An item buyers give to sellers when they want to purchase goods and services |
| **Unit of account** | The yardstick people use to post prices and record debts |
| **Store of value** | An item people can use to transfer purchasing power from the present to the future |
| **Commodity money** | Money that takes the form of a commodity with intrinsic value, e.g. gold coins |
| **Fiat money** | Money without intrinsic value, used as money because of government decree, e.g. a US dollar bill |
| **Money supply (money stock)** | The quantity of money available in the economy |
| **Currency** | The paper bills and coins in the hands of the (non-bank) public |
| **Demand deposits** | Balances in bank accounts that depositors can access on demand by writing a cheque |
| **M1** | Currency, demand deposits, traveller's cheques and other chequeable deposits |
| **M2** | Everything in M1 plus savings deposits, small time deposits, money market mutual funds and a few minor categories |
| **Central bank** | An institution that oversees the banking system and regulates the money supply |
| **Monetary policy** | The setting of the money supply by policymakers in the central bank |
| **Federal Reserve (Fed)** | The central bank of the US |
| **Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)** | The Board of Governors plus presidents of some regional Fed banks; decides monetary policy |
| **Fractional reserve banking** | A system in which banks keep a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend out the rest |
| **Reserve requirements** | Regulations on the minimum amount of reserves banks must hold against deposits |
| **Reserve ratio ($R$)** | The fraction of deposits that banks hold as reserves; total reserves as a percentage of total deposits |
| **Excess reserves** | Reserves held above the required minimum — the money the bank can lend out |
| **T-account** | A simplified accounting statement showing a bank's assets and liabilities |

# 2.2 Monetary Policy and the Interest Rate

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Fed's three tools of monetary control

| Tool | What it is | To increase the money supply | To reduce it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Open-market operations (OMOs)** | The purchase and sale of US government bonds by the Fed | The Fed **buys** government bonds, paying with new dollars | The Fed **sells** government bonds, taking dollars out of circulation |
| **Reserve requirements (RR)** | The minimum reserves banks must hold against deposits (2.1) | The Fed **reduces** RR | The Fed **raises** RR |
| **The discount rate** | The interest rate on loans the Fed makes to banks | The Fed **lowers** the discount rate | The Fed **raises** the discount rate |

Each works through the banking system rather than directly on the public.

**Open-market operations.** When the Fed buys bonds it pays with new dollars, which are deposited in banks and so increase reserves; banks use those reserves to make loans, and the money supply expands. Selling bonds runs the same process in reverse. OMOs are easy to conduct, and they are the Fed's **monetary policy tool of choice**.

**Reserve requirements.** These affect how much money banks can create by making loans. Lowering RR means banks make more loans from each dollar of reserves, which increases the money multiplier and the money supply; raising RR works in reverse. The Fed **rarely** uses reserve requirements to control the money supply, because frequent changes disrupt banking.

**The discount rate.** When banks are running low on reserves they may borrow reserves from the Fed. A lower discount rate encourages banks to borrow more reserves, which they can then lend on, increasing the money supply; a higher rate discourages it. If there is no crisis the Fed rarely uses discount lending — the Fed is a **lender of last resort**.

## The federal funds rate

On any given day, banks with insufficient reserves can borrow from banks with excess reserves. The interest rate on these loans is the **federal funds rate**. The FOMC uses open-market operations to **target** it.

To raise the federal funds rate the Fed sells government bonds. That removes reserves from the banking system, which reduces the supply of federal funds, and the federal funds rate rises.

The federal funds rate matters far beyond the interbank market because many interest rates are **highly correlated**: changes in the federal funds rate cause changes in other rates, and so have a big impact.

## The theory of liquidity preference

The **theory of liquidity preference** is a simple theory of the interest rate, denoted $r$: **$r$ adjusts to balance the supply of and demand for money.**

- The **money supply** is assumed to be fixed by the central bank and does not depend on the interest rate. It equals currency (cash) plus demand deposits.
- **Money demand** reflects how much wealth people want to hold in liquid form.

Suppose household wealth includes only two assets: **money**, which is liquid but pays no interest, and **bonds**, which pay interest but are not as liquid. A household's money demand is then simply its preference for liquidity — for holding the asset it can spend immediately, at the cost of the interest it gives up.

The variables that influence money demand are **$Y$, $r$ and $P$** — real income, the interest rate and the price level.

*Worked example.* Suppose real income $Y$ rises. Households want to buy more goods and services, so they need more money; to get it, they attempt to sell some of their bonds. An **increase in $Y$ causes an increase in money demand**, other things equal.

*Worked example.* When the Federal Reserve purchases bonds, what happens to the price of bonds in the open market? **The price of bonds rises**, because the purchase of bonds increases the money supply, which decreases the interest rate. A free-response answer here is expected to include a correctly labelled money-market graph showing that fall in $r$; the content of that graph is exactly the liquidity-preference model above — a money supply fixed by the central bank, and $r$ moving to clear the market.

## Monetary policy in the two gaps

The guide compresses each case into a chain, and the intermediate steps are the substance of it.

**Recessionary gap:** lower FR and lower RRR and buy government bonds — all three tools at once — so the money supply increases, the interest rate decreases, investment increases, and **aggregate demand increases (shifts right)**.

**Inflationary gap:** raise FR and raise RRR and sell government bonds, so the money supply decreases, the interest rate increases, investment decreases, and aggregate demand decreases (shifts left).

The guide prints "shift left" against both chains; the recessionary one must shift **right**, since the same guide states that an increase in aggregate demand shifts the curve right.

## What monetary expansion actually moves

**Monetary expansionary policy only shifts AD.** When the money supply increases and the interest rate falls:

- **Investment increases**, because the cost of borrowing falls
- **Consumption increases**, because saving falls
- **Exports increase**, because the currency depreciates and exports become cheaper (6)

All three are components of aggregate demand, which is why the whole effect appears as a shift of AD and not of aggregate supply.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Open-market operations (OMOs)** | The purchase and sale of US government bonds by the Fed; the Fed's monetary policy tool of choice |
| **Discount rate** | The interest rate on loans the Fed makes to banks |
| **Lender of last resort** | The Fed's role in lending to banks, used rarely and in crisis |
| **Federal funds rate** | The interest rate on overnight loans between banks with excess reserves and banks with insufficient reserves; targeted by the FOMC through OMOs |
| **Theory of liquidity preference** | A simple theory of the interest rate: $r$ adjusts to balance the supply of and demand for money |
| **Money demand** | How much wealth people want to hold in liquid form; influenced by $Y$, $r$ and $P$ |

# 3.1 Fiscal Policy and Aggregate Demand

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What fiscal policy is

**Fiscal policy** is the setting of the level of government spending and taxation by government policymakers. Where monetary policy is run by the central bank (2.1), fiscal policy is run by the government itself, and it works on aggregate demand through the two instruments it controls.

| Policy | Instruments | Effect on AD |
|---|---|---|
| **Expansionary fiscal policy** | An increase in $G$ and/or a decrease in $T$ | Shifts AD **right** |
| **Contractionary fiscal policy** | A decrease in $G$ and/or an increase in $T$ | Shifts AD **left** |

Fiscal policy then has **two effects on AD** that pull in opposite directions: the multiplier effect makes the shift larger than the initial change, and the crowding-out effect makes it smaller.

## The marginal propensity to consume

The **marginal propensity to consume (MPC)** is the fraction of extra income that households consume rather than save. If MPC $= 0.8$ and income rises by \$100, consumption rises by \$80.

$$\text{MPC} = \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta \text{Income}} \qquad \text{MPC} + \text{MPS} = 1 \qquad \frac{\Delta C + \Delta S}{\Delta \text{Income}} = 1$$

The second and third statements say the same thing: every extra pound or dollar of income is either consumed or saved, so the two propensities must add to one.

*Worked example.* In year 1 Adam earns \$1,000 and saves \$100. In year 2 he gets a \$500 raise, so he earns \$1,500, and out of that \$1,500 he saves \$200. What is his MPC out of the \$500 raise? Work only with the *changes*: saving rose by $\$200 - \$100 = \$100$, so consumption rose by $\$500 - \$100 = \$400$, and

$$\text{MPC} = \frac{400}{500} = 0.80$$

Work with the changes, not with the totals.

## The multiplier effect

The **multiplier effect** is the additional shifts in aggregate demand that result when fiscal policy increases income and thereby increases consumer spending. Because the households who receive the government's spending go on to spend a fraction MPC of it, and the next recipients spend a fraction of that, **each \$1 increase in $G$ can generate more than a \$1 increase in aggregate demand**. The same is true for the other components of GDP, not just for government purchases.

The size of the multiplier is fixed by the MPC:

$$\text{multiplier} = \frac{1}{1 - \text{MPC}}$$

*Worked example.* The economy is in a recession and policymakers want to increase aggregate demand by \$600 billion. The MPC is 0.75 and there is no crowding out. What should the government do? The multiplier is $1/(1-0.75) = 4$, so the required increase in spending is

$$\frac{\$600\text{bn}}{4} = \$150 \text{ billion.}$$

Spending \$600 billion would overshoot by a factor of four; spending \$2,400 billion multiplies when it should divide.

## The crowding-out effect

The **crowding-out effect** is the offset that arises because a fiscal expansion raises the interest rate. The guide's chain runs: $G$ rises, so AD rises, so the price level rises, which shifts the money demand curve rightwards, and so $r$ rises. A higher $r$ **reduces investment**, which reduces the net increase in aggregate demand. So the size of the AD shift may be smaller than the initial fiscal expansion.

*Worked example.* Malaysia's economy is in a recession and its government currently has a balanced budget.

**(a) Identify a specific fiscal policy action to address the recession.** An increase in government spending, a decrease in taxes, or an increase in transfer payments — any one of the three is a valid answer, and the question asks for one *specific* action, so name it.

**(b) How will that action affect the real interest rate? Explain.** The **real interest rate will increase**. The explanation the mark scheme wants is the borrowing route: the government was running a balanced budget, so financing the expansion means borrowing, and **government borrowing increases the demand for loanable funds** (equivalently, it decreases the supply of loanable funds), pushing the real interest rate up.

That rise in $r$ is crowding out seen from the loanable-funds side, and it is the step that connects fiscal policy to the exchange rate in 6.

## Changes in taxes

A **tax cut increases households' take-home pay**. Households respond by spending a portion of this extra income, which shifts AD to the right. The size of the shift depends on the multiplier and the crowding-out effect, and on one further factor: **whether households perceive the tax cut to be temporary or permanent**. A permanent tax cut causes a bigger increase in consumption — and so a bigger shift in the AD curve — than a temporary one, because households treat it as a lasting addition to their income rather than a one-off.

*Worked example.* The economy is in recession, and a congresswoman suggests increasing spending to stimulate aggregate demand while at the same time raising taxes to pay for it. This combination is best described as **mediocre and contradictory**: the spending increase pushes AD right while the tax increase pushes AD left, so the two instruments of fiscal policy are being used against each other.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Fiscal policy** | The setting of the level of government spending and taxation by government policymakers |
| **Expansionary fiscal policy** | An increase in $G$ and/or a decrease in $T$; shifts AD right |
| **Contractionary fiscal policy** | A decrease in $G$ and/or an increase in $T$; shifts AD left |
| **Multiplier effect** | The additional shifts in AD that result when fiscal policy increases income and thereby increases consumer spending |
| **Marginal propensity to consume (MPC)** | The fraction of extra income that households consume rather than save, $\Delta C / \Delta \text{Income}$ |
| **Crowding-out effect** | The reduction in investment caused by the rise in $r$ that a fiscal expansion produces, which reduces the net increase in aggregate demand |

# 3.2 Fiscal Policy, Aggregate Supply and the Government Budget

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The short run works mainly through demand

Most economists believe the **short-run effects of fiscal policy mainly work through aggregate demand** — the multiplier and crowding-out story of 3.1. The aggregate supply effects below are real, but they are slower and more contested, and that distinction is itself examinable.

## Tax rates and aggregate supply

A **cut in the tax rate gives workers an incentive to work more**, so it might increase the quantity of goods and services supplied and shift AS to the right. People who believe this effect is large are called **supply-siders**.

*Worked example.* Which statement would supply-side economists **disagree** with?

- "Tax changes cause shifts in aggregate supply that work **against** shifts in aggregate demand, thus reducing the effect of the tax change on real GDP." — **This is the one they reject.** Their whole position is that the supply-side response reinforces the tax change rather than working against it.
- "A tax cut is likely to increase aggregate supply by boosting saving, investment and capital accumulation." — supply-siders agree.
- "A tax increase is likely to decrease aggregate supply by decreasing after-tax wages and thus providing disincentives to work." — supply-siders agree; this is the incentive argument in reverse.
- "A tax cut is likely to increase aggregate supply by providing greater rewards for risk taking." — supply-siders agree.

## Government purchases and aggregate supply

Government purchases might affect AS as well as AD. If the government increases spending on roads, better roads may increase business productivity, which increases the quantity of goods and services supplied and shifts AS to the right. This effect is **probably more relevant in the long run**: it takes time to build the new roads and put them into use.

The same logic explains which policies raise long-run growth.

*Worked example.* An increase in which of the following would be most likely to increase long-run growth: pension payments, unemployment compensation, subsidies to businesses for purchases of capital goods, or tariffs on imported capital goods? **Subsidies to businesses for purchases of capital goods.** They add to the economy's productive capacity, in the same way better roads do. Pensions and unemployment compensation are transfers that support incomes without adding capital, and a tariff on imported capital goods raises the price of exactly the equipment that would have expanded capacity.

## Budget balance, deficits and the national debt

The budget is **balanced** when tax revenue equals government spending. If the budget is in **surplus** in a financial year, the government is able to repay money it has borrowed in previous years.

The **national debt** is the accumulated total of past government borrowing — the stock of government debt outstanding at a point in time.

The distinction the guide insists on is between **stock and flow**:

| Quantity | Type | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| **National debt** | A **stock** | The total outstanding at a point in time |
| **Budget balance** | A **flow** | The gap between revenue and spending over one financial year |

A **budget deficit** therefore shows the **increase in the national debt that occurs in one year**. A country can run a deficit and still have a small debt, or run a surplus while carrying a large one; the two answer different questions.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Supply-siders** | People who believe the effect of tax cuts on aggregate supply — through greater incentive to work — is large |
| **Budget surplus** | A financial year in which the government is able to repay money borrowed in previous years |
| **Budget deficit** | The increase in the national debt that occurs in one year; a flow |
| **National debt** | The accumulated total of past government borrowing; the stock of government debt outstanding at a point in time |

# 4 Free Trade

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Interdependence

Countries trade because they are interdependent, and the two directions of that trade have precise names.

- **Exports** — goods produced domestically and sold abroad; *to export* means to sell domestically produced goods abroad
- **Imports** — goods produced abroad and sold domestically; *to import* means to purchase goods produced in other countries

## Absolute advantage

**Absolute advantage** is the ability to produce a good **using fewer inputs** than another producer.

*Worked example.* Producing a ton of wheat uses **10 labour hours in the US** against **25 in Japan**, so the **US has an absolute advantage in wheat**. If each country has an absolute advantage in one good and specialises in that good, then **both countries can gain from trade** — each spends its hours where those hours go furthest, and the two swap the results.

## Comparative advantage

**Comparative advantage** is the ability to produce a good at a **lower opportunity cost** than another producer. The crucial point, and the one exams test hardest, is that **absolute advantage is not necessary for comparative advantage**. A country that is worse at producing everything in absolute terms still gives up less of one good to make another than its trading partner does, and that difference is enough to make specialisation and trade worthwhile for both. This is why the jobs argument of 5.2 fails: a country needs only a comparative advantage, not an absolute one, to have a viable export industry.

The two concepts answer different questions: absolute advantage asks *how many inputs does this take?*, comparative advantage asks *what else could those inputs have made?*

## The benefits of international trade

Free trade delivers a cluster of benefits, and they are worth reading as a chain rather than a list — competition drives prices down, and access to bigger markets lets firms produce at a scale that lowers costs further.

- **Increased competition**
- **Lower prices**
- **Greater choice**
- **Access to larger markets**
- **Acquisition of resources**
- **Economies of scale**
- **More efficient resource allocation**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Exports** | Goods produced domestically and sold abroad |
| **Imports** | Goods produced abroad and sold domestically |
| **Absolute advantage** | The ability to produce a good using fewer inputs than another producer |
| **Comparative advantage** | The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer; absolute advantage is not necessary for it |

markdown:
# 5.1 World Prices, Tariffs and Quotas

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The world price and the domestic price

Two prices decide whether a country exports or imports a good.

- $P_W$ — the **world price** of a good; the price that prevails in world markets
- $P_D$ — the **domestic price** without trade

| Condition | What it means | Under free trade |
|---|---|---|
| $P_D < P_W$ | The country **has** a comparative advantage in the good | The country **exports** it |
| $P_D > P_W$ | The country does **not** have a comparative advantage | The country **imports** it |

Comparing the two prices is what reveals where the comparative advantage of 4 lies.

## The small economy assumption

A **small economy** is a **price taker** in world markets: its actions have no effect on $P_W$. This is not always true — especially not for the US — but it simplifies the analysis without changing its lessons.

When a small economy engages in free trade, $P_W$ is the **only relevant price**, and the reason is arbitrage on both sides of the market:

- No seller would accept less than $P_W$, since she could sell the good for $P_W$ in world markets.
- No buyer would pay more than $P_W$, since he could buy the good for $P_W$ in world markets.

## Further benefits of international trade

Beyond the benefits listed in 4, the guide adds four that bear directly on why restricting trade is costly:

- Consumers enjoy **increased variety** of goods.
- Producers sell to a **larger market**, and may achieve **lower costs** by producing on a larger scale.
- **Competition from abroad may reduce the market power of domestic firms**, which would increase total welfare.
- Trade **enhances the flow of ideas** and facilitates the spread of technology around the world.

## Tariffs

A **tariff** is a **tax on imports**. In general, the price facing domestic buyers and sellers becomes

$$P_W + T$$

so the tariff raises the price inside the country above the world price by exactly the amount of the tax. A tariff **creates revenue for the government**.

## Import quotas

An **import quota** is a **quantitative limit on imports** of a good. It mostly has the same effects as a tariff: it **raises the price and reduces the quantity of imports**. The difference is who collects the gain.

| | Tariff | Quota |
|---|---|---|
| Effect on price | Raises it | Raises it |
| Effect on quantity of imports | Reduces it | Reduces it |
| Who gains the extra revenue | **The government**, as tariff revenue | **The foreign producers** of the imported goods, who can sell at the higher price |

A government can recover that gain by **auctioning licences to import**, capturing the foreign producers' profit as revenue instead.

## Other barriers to trade

- **Export subsidies** — if a government subsidises domestic production, this gives its producers an unfair advantage over competitors.
- **Administrative barriers** — making it more difficult to trade, for example by imposing minimum environmental standards.

## Case study: US tariffs on Chinese goods

The case concerns the statutory four-year review of the tariffs imposed by the Trump administration in 2018 and 2019 on thousands of imports from China, valued at around \$370 billion at the time, and imposed as a bargaining chip for trade talks with Beijing. The text reports that much of the cost of those tariffs was passed on to US consumers and businesses, that US inflation had by then eased, and that the review might add more imports from China to the tariffs.

**(a) Define the term tariff.** A **tax on imports**.

**(b) Explain why a tariff contributes to inflation in the US.** A tariff **increases the prices of imported goods**, which worsens inflation in the US. Follow it through both groups affected:

- **Households** face a higher cost of living and lose purchasing power when the prices of the items they buy — food, utilities, gasoline — increase.
- **Companies** lose purchasing power when prices rise for the inputs used in production: raw materials such as coal and crude oil, intermediate products such as flour and steel, and finished machinery.

In response, companies typically **raise the prices of their products or services to offset** the increase, meaning consumers absorb these price rises. This is **cost-push inflation** — inflation driven from the cost side rather than by demand.

**(c) Using a tariff diagram, explain the effects of adding more Chinese imports to the tariffs on producers, consumers and governments in both countries.** The answer key leaves this part blank, so build the answer from what the guide states about how a tariff works.

| Stakeholder | Effect |
|---|---|
| **US consumers** | Pay $P_W + T$ rather than $P_W$, and absorb the price rises firms pass on |
| **US producers competing with imports** | Protected from foreign competition by the higher price, which is the basis of the jobs argument in 5.2 |
| **US firms using imported inputs** | Hurt, since they buy imported goods as raw materials at the tariff-inclusive price |
| **US government** | Gains tariff revenue |
| **Chinese producers** | Sell less, because the tariff reduces the quantity of imports; the text describes the tariffs as being used to hurt China's lower-end manufacturing industries |
| **Chinese government** | Objects, and may retaliate — protection risks a trade war |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **World price ($P_W$)** | The price of a good that prevails in world markets |
| **Domestic price ($P_D$)** | The price of a good in the country without trade |
| **Small economy** | An economy that is a price taker in world markets; its actions have no effect on $P_W$ |
| **Tariff** | A tax on imports; the price facing domestic buyers and sellers becomes $P_W + T$ |
| **Import quota** | A quantitative limit on imports of a good |
| **Export subsidy** | A government subsidy to domestic production that gives producers an unfair advantage over competitors |
| **Administrative barriers** | Measures making it more difficult to trade, e.g. imposing minimum environmental standards |
| **Cost-push inflation** | Inflation arising when higher input prices lead firms to raise the prices of their products |

# 5.2 Arguments for Protectionism and Trade Agreements

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Five arguments are made for restricting trade. Each has a standard economists' response, and the exam expects the pair, not the argument alone.

## 1. The jobs argument

**The claim:** trade destroys jobs in the industries that compete against imports.

**Economists' response:** total unemployment does not rise as imports rise, because job losses from imports are offset by job gains in export industries. And even if all goods could be produced more cheaply abroad, the country need only have a **comparative advantage** — not an absolute one (4) — to have a viable export industry and to gain from trade.

## 2. The national security argument

**The claim:** an industry vital to national security should be protected from foreign competition, to prevent dependence on imports that could be disrupted during wartime.

**Economists' response:** fine, as long as policy is based on **true security needs**. The danger is that producers exaggerate their own importance to national security in order to obtain protection from foreign competition.

## 3. The infant-industry argument

**The claim:** a new industry needs temporary protection until it is mature and can compete with foreign firms.

**Economists' response:** it is difficult for a government to determine which industries will eventually be able to compete, and whether the benefits of establishing them exceed the cost to consumers of restricting imports. Besides, **if a firm will be profitable in the long run, it should be willing to incur temporary losses**.

## 4. The unfair-competition argument

**The claim:** producers argue that their competitors in another country have an unfair advantage, for example because of government subsidies.

**Economists' response:** great — then we can import extra-cheap products subsidised by the other country's taxpayers. **The gains to our consumers will exceed the losses to our producers.**

## 5. The protection-as-bargaining-chip argument

**The claim:** the threat of protection can win concessions. The US can threaten to limit imports of French wine unless France lifts its quotas on American beef.

**Economists' response:** suppose France refuses. The US must then choose between two bad options:

- **(A)** restrict imports from France, which **reduces welfare in the US**; or
- **(B)** don't restrict imports, which **reduces US credibility**.

The threat is only useful while it is not tested, which is the weakness of using trade policy as leverage.

## Trade agreements

A country can liberalise trade with **unilateral reductions** in its own trade restrictions, or with **multilateral agreements** with other nations.

| Agreement | Date | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA)** | 1993 | |
| **General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)** | Ongoing | |
| **World Trade Organization (WTO)** | Established 1995 | Enforces trade agreements and resolves disputes; 164 members by 2016 |

The **WTO's objective** is to facilitate fair, transparent and open global trade. Its **functions** balance economic growth with dispute resolution and support for developing nations.

## Case study: discussing a decision to keep tariffs in place

The case asks students to *discuss* the Biden administration's decision to keep the tariffs in place, given that blacklist sanctions target China's high-tech sectors while the tariffs hit its lower-end manufacturing industries. A "discuss" answer needs both sides.

**For protectionism**

- Free trade destroys jobs in US industries that compete with imports; tariffs protect domestic producers and keep the jobs for US people.
- An industry vital to national security — the high-tech sectors, for instance — should be protected from foreign competition, to prevent dependence on imports that could be disrupted during wartime.
- A new industry may argue for temporary protection until it is mature and can compete with foreign firms.
- Producers argue their competitors in another country have an unfair advantage, for example because of government subsidies.
- Tariffs **gain government revenue**.

**Against protectionism**

- **Free trade increases economic growth.** The US International Trade Commission estimated that NAFTA could increase US economic growth by **0.1%–0.5% a year**.
- **A more dynamic business climate.** Without free trade agreements, countries often protected their domestic industries and businesses; tariffs and other protection often made them stagnant and uncompetitive on the global market. With the protection removed, they became motivated to become true global competitors.
- **Lower government spending.** Many governments subsidise local industries; after a trade agreement removes those subsidies, the funds can be put to better use.
- **Technology transfer.** Local companies gain access to the latest technologies from their multinational partners. As local economies grow, so do job opportunities, and multinational companies provide job training to local employees.
- Protection **hurts domestic consumers and manufacturers** who use imported goods as raw materials.
- It **may arouse a trade war and retaliation**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **The jobs argument** | The claim that trade destroys jobs in industries competing against imports |
| **The national security argument** | The claim that an industry vital to national security should be protected to prevent dependence on imports that could be disrupted in wartime |
| **The infant-industry argument** | The claim that a new industry needs temporary protection until it is mature enough to compete with foreign firms |
| **The unfair-competition argument** | The claim that foreign competitors have an unfair advantage, e.g. from government subsidies |
| **The protection-as-bargaining-chip argument** | The claim that threatening to restrict imports can force another country to lift its own restrictions |
| **Unilateral liberalisation** | A country reducing its own trade restrictions by itself |
| **Multilateral agreement** | Trade liberalisation agreed with other nations |
| **NAFTA** | North American Free Trade Agreement, 1993 |
| **GATT** | General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, ongoing |
| **WTO** | World Trade Organization, established 1995; enforces trade agreements and resolves disputes, with 164 members by 2016 |

# 6 The Foreign Exchange Market and Exchange Rate Systems

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What moves net exports

Six variables influence net exports:

- Consumers' **preferences** for foreign and domestic goods
- **Prices** of goods at home and abroad
- **Incomes** of consumers at home and abroad
- The **exchange rates** at which foreign currency trades for domestic currency
- **Transportation costs**
- **Government policies** — the tariffs, quotas and other barriers of 5.1

*Worked example.* The exchange rate moves from 1 USD = 6.8 RMB to 1 USD = 7.2 RMB. The **dollar appreciates**, so:

- **US exports decrease** — US products are now more expensive to foreign buyers
- **US imports increase** — one dollar buys more foreign goods
- **US net exports decrease**

Read the same move from the other side: the **RMB depreciates**, so China's **exports increase, imports decrease, and net exports increase**. One exchange rate movement always tells two opposite stories.

## Trade surpluses and deficits

**Net exports (NX) measure the imbalance in a country's trade in goods and services.**

| Position | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Trade deficit** | An excess of imports over exports |
| **Trade surplus** | An excess of exports over imports |
| **Balanced trade** | Exports equal imports |

## The flow of capital

The flow of capital abroad takes two forms.

**Foreign direct investment** — domestic residents actively manage the foreign investment, as when McDonald's opens a fast-food outlet in Moscow. Each side has its own motive: the foreign government wants it because it **creates job opportunities and promotes technological advancement** in the host economy, and the domestic government wants it for **efficiency**. The guide prints these two motives the other way round; that is an error — on the guide's own definition the investment is managed from home and lands abroad, so it is the foreign economy that gains the jobs and the technology.

**Foreign portfolio investment** — domestic residents purchase foreign stocks or bonds, supplying "loanable funds" to a foreign firm. The investor here is a lender, not a manager, which is the whole difference between the two forms.

## The nominal exchange rate

The **nominal exchange rate** is the rate at which one country's currency trades for another. The guide's convention is to express **all exchange rates as foreign currency per unit of domestic currency**, so a bigger number always means a stronger domestic currency.

- **Appreciation** ("strengthening") — an **increase** in the value of a currency, measured by the amount of foreign currency it can buy
- **Depreciation** ("weakening") — a **decrease** in the value of a currency, measured the same way

*Worked example.* Which is likely to occur following a depreciation of the US dollar? **US exports will increase.** A weaker dollar makes US goods cheaper to foreign buyers, which is the export half of the appreciation example above run in reverse.

## Why the currency demand and supply curves slope as they do

The diagrams themselves are not reproduced here, but the guide states the reasoning behind each slope, and the reasoning is what is examined.

- **The demand curve slopes downward:** when the USD depreciates, US goods are cheaper, so the **quantity of USD demanded increases**.
- **The supply curve slopes upward:** when the USD appreciates, UK products are cheaper, so the **quantity of USD supplied increases** — holders of dollars offer them in exchange for the now-cheaper foreign goods.

## Reading a currency market

A set of practice questions works from a figure showing the market for **pounds** priced in dollars, with equilibrium at **\$2 for £1**. The figure has not survived into these notes, but each question can be answered from that equilibrium and from the definitions above.

**Which statement is true?** *At the equilibrium exchange rate, the pound price of \$1 is £0.5.* The two quotations are reciprocals of each other: if £1 costs \$2, then \$1 costs £0.5.

**At the price of \$2 for £1:** *the quantity of pounds supplied equals the quantity demanded.* That is what makes it the equilibrium — not that US exports to Britain must equal US imports from Britain, and not that the rate is unstable.

**A leftward shift of the demand curve** *might be caused by a major recession in the United States.* Incomes of consumers at home are one of the variables that move net exports: in a recession, Americans buy fewer British goods and so demand fewer pounds.

**A rightward shift of the supply curve** *would appreciate the dollar and might be caused by a significant rise of real interest rates in the United States.* Higher US real interest rates draw funds towards dollar assets, so more pounds are offered in exchange for dollars; with more pounds supplied, each dollar buys more pounds, which is precisely what appreciation means.

*Worked example.* If the central bank of Country Z wishes to **increase the value of its currency** on foreign exchange markets, it can **raise interest rates in Country Z**. Note what does not work: buying the currencies of other countries, increasing the domestic money supply (which lowers the interest rate — 2.2), or raising tariffs.

*Worked example — the fiscal-policy chain, continued from 3.1.* Malaysia and Japan are trading partners with flexible exchange rates. Malaysia's expansionary fiscal policy raises its **real interest rate**, so on a correctly labelled graph of the foreign exchange market for the **ringgit relative to the yen**, the higher return attracts foreign funds and the **ringgit appreciates**. As a result **Malaysia's imports increase**, because the appreciation makes **Japanese goods relatively less expensive** than they were before. Notice that this runs opposite to monetary expansion, which lowers the interest rate and depreciates the currency (2.2).

## Exchange rate systems

| System | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed (pegged)** | The government seeks to keep the value of a currency fixed against another currency | **Saudi Arabia** — the riyal is pegged at 3.75 SAR per USD |
| **Floating** | The government does not intervene in the foreign exchange market, but allows market forces to determine the level of the currency | **United States** — the dollar fluctuates on forex markets; **Eurozone** — the euro floats freely |
| **Managed float ("dirty float")** | An exchange rate system that allows a nation's central bank to intervene occasionally in foreign exchange markets, to change the direction of the currency's float and/or reduce the amount of currency volatility | **China** — the People's Bank of China allows the yuan to trade within a controlled band; **Brazil** — the central bank sometimes intervenes; **Singapore** — the Monetary Authority manages the SGD against a trade-weighted basket of currencies |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Net exports (NX)** | The imbalance in a country's trade in goods and services |
| **Trade deficit** | An excess of imports over exports |
| **Trade surplus** | An excess of exports over imports |
| **Balanced trade** | When exports equal imports |
| **Foreign direct investment** | Investment abroad that domestic residents actively manage, e.g. McDonald's opening an outlet in Moscow |
| **Foreign portfolio investment** | Domestic residents purchasing foreign stocks or bonds, supplying "loanable funds" to a foreign firm |
| **Nominal exchange rate** | The rate at which one country's currency trades for another, expressed as foreign currency per unit of domestic currency |
| **Appreciation (strengthening)** | An increase in the value of a currency as measured by the amount of foreign currency it can buy |
| **Depreciation (weakening)** | A decrease in the value of a currency as measured by the amount of foreign currency it can buy |
| **Fixed exchange rate system** | A system in which the government seeks to keep the currency's value fixed against another currency |
| **Floating exchange rate system** | A system in which the government does not intervene and market forces determine the currency's level |
| **Managed float (dirty float)** | A system allowing the central bank to intervene occasionally to change the direction of the float and/or reduce volatility |

# 1 Why Nations Trade: Absolute and Comparative Advantage

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

No country can effectively produce everything it needs, so nations trade with one another. Trade makes it possible for a country to have access to products and services that it is unable to manufacture at home. That is the starting point for everything else in this unit: trade is not a favour one country does another, it is a way of getting hold of goods your own economy cannot supply — or cannot supply cheaply.

Two ideas explain who ends up producing what.

## Absolute advantage

A nation has an **absolute advantage** if it can manufacture a good with less labour and capital than another nation. It is a straight comparison of productive power: for the same inputs, who gets more out?

Take Japan and Sweden. Japan has an absolute advantage in the camera industry, and Sweden has an absolute advantage in making cars. Japan makes more cameras and Sweden makes more cars, so by trading they can both benefit from each other while making a profit. Each country hands over the good it is better at producing and receives the good the other is better at producing, and neither has to run an industry it is poor at.

## Comparative advantage

Absolute advantage only settles the easy case, where each country is plainly better at a different good. The idea that decides the general case is opportunity cost.

A country has a **comparative advantage** when it can produce a good at a lower **opportunity cost** — what it gives up to produce that good — than another country. The question is no longer "who produces more?" but "who gives up less to produce it?"

New Zealand may produce fruit more efficiently than industrial goods, so it should focus on fruit and trade for industrial goods. The worked comparison uses these output figures, in tons, for China and New Zealand.

| Country | Fruit | Industrial goods |
|---|---|---|
| China | 35 | 21 |
| New Zealand | 30 | 6 |

### Working out the opportunity cost of fruit

The opportunity cost of one ton of fruit is the industrial goods given up per ton of fruit, so it is the industrial-goods figure divided by the fruit figure.

$$\text{China: } \frac{21}{35} = 0.6$$

So for every fruit, China sacrifices 0.6 industrial goods that could have been produced.

$$\text{New Zealand: } \frac{6}{30} = 0.2$$

So for every fruit, New Zealand only sacrifices 0.2 industrial goods that could have been produced.

### Working out the opportunity cost of industrial goods

Turn the ratio the other way up. The opportunity cost of one ton of industrial goods is the fruit given up per ton of industrial goods.

$$\text{China: } \frac{35}{21} = 1.67$$

For every industrial good produced, China sacrifices 1.67 fruits that could have been produced.

$$\text{New Zealand: } \frac{30}{6} = 5$$

For every industrial good produced, New Zealand sacrifices 5 fruits that could have been produced.

### Reading the result

New Zealand has a higher opportunity cost when producing industrial goods — 5 fruits given up against China's 1.67 — so trading fruit for industrial goods will benefit them. The same comparison run on fruit points the same way: New Zealand gives up only 0.2 industrial goods per ton of fruit where China gives up 0.6.

The pattern to hold on to is that the two calculations are the same table read in two directions, and a country's comparative advantage lies in the good with the **lower** opportunity cost figure.

## How trade benefits nations

**Increased efficiency.** Countries specialise in what they do best, which leads to higher global output. If New Zealand puts its resources into the good it sacrifices least to make, and China does the same, the same resources across the two countries produce more in total than they would if each tried to supply itself.

## Potential downsides of free trade

Free trade is not costless, and three costs stand out.

- **Job losses.** Industries that cannot compete may shrink — for example, U.S. manufacturing moving overseas.
- **Dependency.** Over-reliance on imports can be risky, for example when shortages occur during global crises. A country that has stopped making a good has no domestic supply to fall back on.
- **Environmental and labour concerns.** Some countries may exploit workers or natural resources to cut costs.

These downsides are the reason the next part of the course exists: they are what governments cite when they restrict trade.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Absolute advantage** | A nation has an absolute advantage if it can manufacture a good with less labour and capital than another nation |
| **Comparative advantage** | A country has a comparative advantage when it can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country |
| **Opportunity cost** | What a country gives up in order to produce a good |
| **Increased efficiency** | The benefit of trade by which countries specialise in what they do best, leading to higher global output |

markdown:
# 2 World Price and Comparative Advantage

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Opportunity-cost tables tell you where a country's comparative advantage lies. Prices tell you the same thing more directly. Comparing a country's own price with the price the rest of the world charges is enough to say which way a good will move once trade opens.

## The two prices

$P_W$ is the **world price** of a good, the price that prevails in world markets. $P_D$ is the **domestic price** without trade — what the good costs inside the country before any trading takes place.

## The rule

| Comparison | What it means | What happens under free trade |
|---|---|---|
| $P_D < P_W$ | This country has a comparative advantage in the good | The country exports the good |
| $P_D > P_W$ | This country does not have a comparative advantage in the good | The country imports the good |

The logic runs through cost. A country that can already supply the good more cheaply than the world does is the low-opportunity-cost producer, so it has the comparative advantage and sells outward. A country whose own price sits above the world price is the expensive producer, so it buys from abroad instead.

## Worked case: electric vehicles

Take the case where $P_D > P_W$ in the EV cars industry. The domestic price is the higher of the two, so imports at the cheaper world price are encouraged. American buyers who were paying the domestic price now have a cheaper source, and they take it.

Two effects follow, and the guide shows both on a graph of this market:

- The **price decreases**, because domestic sellers now have to compete with the imported price.
- The **total surplus increases**, so the United States gains overall from the trade.

The second point is worth holding on to. Trade here is not a transfer where one side's gain is the other's loss: opening the EV market leaves the U.S. with more gains than it had under the higher domestic price. That claim is exactly what protectionist policy disputes, and the next lesson takes up the same EV market with a tariff placed on it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **World price ($P_W$)** | The world price of a good — the price that prevails in world markets |
| **Domestic price ($P_D$)** | The domestic price of a good without trade |

markdown:
# 3 Trade Protectionism

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What protectionism is

**Protectionism** refers to government policies that restrict free trade to shield domestic industries from foreign competition. The target is always the same — imports that undercut home producers — but governments have four different instruments for hitting it, and they do not have the same side effects.

| Method | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Tariffs | Taxes on imports | The U.S. imposes a 247.5% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) |
| Import quotas | Limits on the quantity of imported goods | The EU restricts the number of U.S. steel imports |
| Subsidies | Government payments to domestic firms | India subsidises sugar exports to compete globally |
| Non-tariff barriers | Regulations, standards and bureaucracy | The EU bans hormone-treated U.S. beef, citing health concerns |

## Tariffs

A tariff is a tax on imports, and the U.S. tariff of 247.5% on Chinese EVs makes those cars far more expensive in the American market. Four parties are affected, two of them gaining and two losing.

**In favour.** U.S. producers face less foreign competition, because products from China will be too expensive for consumers, so more of the domestic product will be bought by Americans instead. More business means more production, revenue and employment. The U.S. government also benefits, because the extra money producers pay due to the tariff becomes government revenue, which can later be used to build infrastructure, fund public services and so on.

**Against.** Chinese exporters lose a large part of the American market, because their products become more expensive for American buyers. That means fewer exports and therefore less revenue, production and employment on their side. And U.S. consumers have to pay higher prices, because the Chinese products that were cheaper than domestic ones now carry the tariff. Demand and consumer surplus both decrease.

Note that the tariff runs the previous lesson's EV case backwards. Free trade in EVs pushed the domestic price down and total surplus up; the tariff pushes the price American consumers pay back up and takes consumer surplus away, while moving revenue to domestic producers and to the government.

## Import quotas

A quota limits the quantity of a good that may be imported rather than taxing it. The EU's restriction on the number of U.S. steel imports is an example.

The costs are shortages, higher prices, and no extra revenues for government. That last one is the difference between a quota and a tariff and is worth remembering: a tariff raises the price by collecting a tax, so the government ends up holding the money, whereas a quota raises the price by making the good scarce, so no revenue is collected at all.

## Subsidies

A subsidy is a government payment to domestic firms — India, for example, subsidises sugar exports so its producers can compete globally.

Subsidies support struggling industries and encourage domestic production. Against that, they can lead to overproduction, and they cause trade disputes: the WTO often bans unfair subsidies.

## Non-tariff barriers

These are regulations, standards and bureaucracy that keep a foreign good out without taxing or counting it. The EU's ban on hormone-treated U.S. beef, citing health concerns, is the example — a rule written as a health standard that has the effect of excluding an import.

## Arguments for protectionism

- **Protecting jobs.** Tariffs on steel save U.S. factory jobs.
- **National security.** Protection limits reliance on foreign weapons or food.
- **Preventing unfair competition.** China's state subsidies for EVs are the example — if a foreign government is paying its producers, domestic firms are not competing against a company but against a treasury.

## Arguments against protectionism

- **Higher consumer prices.** Tariffs make imports costlier, and consumers pay the difference.
- **Trade wars.** Tariffs hurt exporters and might encourage them to implement retaliatory tariffs, as China did to the U.S. The first tariff therefore does not settle the matter; it invites a second one aimed back at your own exporters.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Protectionism** | Government policies that restrict free trade to shield domestic industries from foreign competition |
| **Tariffs** | Taxes on imports |
| **Import quotas** | Limits on the quantity of imported goods |
| **Subsidies** | Government payments to domestic firms |
| **Non-tariff barriers** | Regulations, standards and bureaucracy used to restrict imports |
